t: Why You Shouldn't Forget This Powerful Back-To-School Strategy
q: But you also can’t forget one of the most powerful strategies of all.
You see, for all that stuff to work as it should, to get your students to care enough to listen, to motivate them, intrinsically, to want to buy-in, they have to enjoy being there.
So my number one goal those first few days of school isn’t just to lay the groundwork. It’s to get them to love being in my class.
Now, it’s important to point out that you don’t need any special talent or ability to use humor in your classroom.
Humor is everywhere. School is a target-rich environment and kids are inherently funny. They love to laugh and appreciate any attempt to make them smile.
It makes your sky-high standards and expectations, which can be a shock to the system, more palatable. It puts your students at ease during what can be a stressful time for them.

t: When Current Events Remain the Job of Single Departments, Kids Won’t Graduate Understanding the World Well standing-world-well/
q: Kids (and adults!) won’t produce quality, clear thinking unless they know enough things. Knowledge begets critical thinking. Critically thinking is not immaculately conceived.

In order to understand things like US politics, global climate, the rise of automation, or the North Korea security and humanitarian crises, you need to know a lot of things, and such robust knowledge-building can’t happen in a single course or department. I don’t care how many times you talk to kids about critical thinking or how many times you have them argue or pop-up debate on the topics I just mentioned.
Here's the thing: it was my fault. I hadn't given my students a chance to learn enough about the North Korea situation yet.

The improvement was remarkable — students built on one another’s ideas, used Paraphrase Plus, and came much closer to matching what I had originally hoped for several weeks prior. Knowledge begot critical thinking and productive, argumentative discourse.

Something like this need only take 15 minutes maximum of class time each week, and it can take less once students are used to it. Importantly, grading on this should not be intensive. The primary purpose of the assignment is knowledge-building, and the secondary benefits include practice with quantitative reasoning, graph reading, and writing in the content areas.

Of course, there are also secondary benefits when we systematize the inclusion of regular current events articles: our students get the opportunity to read and write more. Since quantity precedes quality, this is no small boon.

Please notice that such ways of thinking devalue the 50% of students who would take advantage of an opportunity. This is something I hope my children's teachers never do, so it's something I won't do. You and I are in the business of providing opportunities, not guaranteeing results.

Teachers should not withhold good opportunities because only some students will complete them; the job is to provide opportunity, not guarantee results.

q: Utility is part of the rationale for an education — I want my daughters and son to be able to earn a living for themselves and their families — but, just like the professor in California was getting at, it is far from the whole.

we need our students to build knowledge, argue, read, write, speak, and listen frequently and with ever greater care and skill because our democratic republic depends on them being knowledgeable and skillful in these areas by the time they're 18.
You ought to become a thoughtful, literate person not just because of what it can do for your life, but because of what it can do for all of our lives.

The public school classroom never ought to be used to teach one's political or religious views as the only way, but it always ought to be a place where we teach and require students to found opinions on strong evidence and clear reasoning.
Like Mr. Miagi asking Daniel to “wax on, wax off,” what we're doing here is building an unconscious bias toward reasoned decision-making.

q: But then, three or four weeks in, things begin to change. Restlessness creeps in. Attitudes develop. Listening takes a nosedive and the room starts buzzing with voices and excitability.
The truth, however, is that slowly, imperceptibly, you’ve fallen into a progression of bad habits.
It can cause you to become complacent. It can cause you to let your guard down, take your foot off the gas, and question—in the far recesses of your mind—why you need to be such a stickler.
And slowly but surely, these small inconsistencies send the message to your new class that you don’t really mean what you say.
The end result is even more misbehavior, scant leverage to do much about it, and every day feeling like the Siege of Bastogne.
So right now, this second, vow to follow your classroom management plan as it's written. Stay true to your promises and high-bar standards.

q: If we're going to improve the quality of writing our students are capable of — an absolutely critical endeavor — then we first need to ensure that our kids have a large amount of writing that they do. Quantity precedes quality.
As I'm identifying these things, I don't mark a single thing on their papers — I'm just populating the Skull and Crossbones list. If I have to put a grade, it's credit / no credit.

For example, placing commas correctly is something that gets harder over time because the kinds of sentences students are trying to create get more complex over time. But capitalizing things doesn't really do that. It's not recursive.
As time progresses, I'll add things as needed. I don't want to create 100 things on this list, but a dozen or two goes a long way.

If a team of athletes wanted to be elite — if they wanted to do hard things — they would certainly be silly to think they'd get there by being sloppy in the most basic elements of their sport. I want all of my students to have the chance now to be held unemotionally accountable for a basic attention to detail by someone who loves them (me). I want them to know that, in truth, details do matter — that it pays to attend to them.
I think this is one reason that parents don't tend to complain about this. The student is free to fix her problems and re-submit.
x: Quantity of writing comes first, but once it is in place a short, responsive list of habitual errors is the cheapest way to lift quality.
Hold the line without marking up papers: return the work with a frownie face, record a zero until the student fixes it, and let the posted list serve as the reference.

t: Cheap Prizes: We Didn’t Get into This for Those
q: The awards, praises, and “favorite teacher” comments are cheap prizes. We did not get into teaching for these things.
That drive to prove himself, to receive external affirmation for what he's doing in the classroom, to be seen as remarkably good at this work: those demons are regulars around here.
And part of that is because public opinion and this year's eval rubric are fickle, here today and changed tomorrow. Like shifting sand dunes, they have impermanence woven into them.
Over a school year, who knows that we could be 1% of the reasons why our students go on to lead flourishing lives?

These don't get tied to merit pay, and they probably won't show up on the end of year test. But they're why we got in; we have to hold to them, even as we pursue the student achievement results our stakeholders desire.

It's these conversations with ourselves, these moments of hard internal interrogation, that keep us on the road to becoming the teachers we always hoped we'd be and staying sane in the process. This is part of the inner work of teaching.

t: 5 Simple Ways To Eliminate Stress From Your Teaching Life
q: Stress is a killer. And not just physically. It can also ruin your teaching career.
The way it works is just before your students arrive for the day, shut your classroom door and allow yourself a few minutes of uninterrupted silence.
Nearly every teacher would benefit by using more of this two-letter word. If fact, if you don’t say no regularly, chances are that you’re overworked and near the end of your rope.

Besides being ineffective, trying to counsel, question, scold, guilt, coax, manipulate, persuade, or otherwise find the perfect words to get students to behave is incredibly burdensome and the most stressful strategy you can use.
Micromanaging, coddling, and over-helping very effectively produces learned helplessness. It dissuades listening and encourages dependence on you.
It also brings tense, negative energy into your classroom that you can't feel, but that visitors experience the moment they walk through your door.
x: Michael Linsin offers five concrete strategies for reducing teacher stress: the 'decide-first' method of consciously committing to calm before students arrive each day; saying no more often, not just to extra duties but…
The 'decide-first' method — consciously committing to stay calm before students arrive, every day — is described as simple but genuinely transformative over time.
Teachers should say no more often, not only to extra responsibilities but to gossip, procrastination, and negative colleagues.
Trying to verbally convince students to behave — counseling, scolding, persuading — is the most burdensome and least effective classroom management strategy.
Shifting full responsibility for independent work onto students, rather than micromanaging or re-teaching, reduces stress and prevents learned helplessness.

q: But there is something about the first day of school that causes many teachers to behave in ways that undermine their best laid plans.
Talk too much and they’ll tune you out. They’ll form a negative impression of you and being in your class, which is the seed from which misbehavior grows.
But using fear, no matter how subtle the undercurrent, to coerce good behavior will only make your job more difficult—because it will very effectively sabotage your relationship with your new class.
They fear disappointing their new class so much that they tiptoe around their classroom management plan. They minimize its importance.
So teach it boldly. Be clear and confident. Show your students through your words, your passion, and your very presence that you will indeed fulfill your every promise.

The mistakes above are particularly insidious because they’re difficult to see in oneself. You look back a week later and think, “I was so prepared, and I did everything I wanted to do, yet why am I struggling?

q: In my experience, these things create challenging circumstances (and many times the challenge lies not in the things but in the ignoring of them), but they don't burn me out. Really, what burns me out is my unrealistic expectations.
This kind of idealism doesn't lead to burnout; rather, it acts as a charm for keeping burnout at bay.
I have to grade everything, and all of that grading has to be done the same way (when, in fact, some of the best teachers grade very pragmatically);
What I've briefly painted here is what many of the best career teachers possess: realistic idealism. That first set of bullet points is about as high-minded as it comes. It is hugely idealistic.
But that bottom list is interesting because, to hold to it, we need to ignore the overly optimistic voices that surround us — those who believe that we can somehow do All The Things.
You can't climb up Mount Everest with your kitchen sink. You can bring only what is required.
x: Burnout is traced to the teacher's own unrealistic expectations rather than to external policy pressure.
Big-picture ideals such as long-term flourishing of students act as a charm against burnout rather than a cause of it.
Pragmatic grading, whole-class feedback and ruthless triage of pointless tasks are presented as marks of the best career teachers.
He calls the combination realistic idealism and says many of the best career teachers possess it.
It requires ignoring both pessimistic voices and the overly optimistic voices that say we can do All The Things.
